Weep for the nation in its present plight,
And for the gloom that shadows future light;
The proud confederate eagle heard the sound,
And in her flight fell prostrate to the ground!

Weep for the loss the country has sustained,
By which her now-dependent lies in chains;
The grief of him who yet the war survived,
The conscript husbands and their weeping wives!

Weep for the seas of blood the battle cost,
And souls that hope had held, forever lost!
The ravaged fields that no recruit restore,
The trees by vengeance blasted to their core!

Weep for the downfall crowning heads and chief,
Who sank bereft of any means of relief;
Who fell beneath the hatchet of their pride,
Then, serpent-like, self-poisoned, drooped and died!

Weep for the downfall of your president,
Who far too late his folly must lament;
Who, dragon-like, did all of heaven assail,
And dragged his friends to limbo with his tail!

Weep o'er the swelling coffers, hollow, void,
Our treasures fled, their every bank destroyed;
Their groundless notes, replete with shame to all,
Awaiting daily their appointed fall,
In quest of profit never to be won,
Then sadly fallen, and forever down!

---

outputs.L2:
Mourn for this nation as it stands today,
And for the darkness looming on its way;
The haughty rebel eagle caught the call,
And in her soaring, tumbled down to fall!

Lament the damages the land endured,
Which leaves her dependent behind bars secured;
The sorrow of the man who lived through strife,
The drafted spouses and each grieving wife!

Grieve for the oceans spilled in battle's toll,
And every hopeful yet forever-lost soul!
The wasted battlefields with none to sow,
Trees split to their roots where wrath did blow!

Weep for the ruin brought on chief and head,
Who dropped with no relief from what had bled;
Who perished by the axe their own pride raised,
Then, snakelike, bit themselves and left the days!

Lament the toppling of your president,
Whose foolishness too late he must repent;
Who, dragon-like, assaulted heaven's height,
And swept his allies down into the night!

Cry over private vaults now emptied bare,
Our riches gone, their banks in ruined despair;
Their worthless notes, a shame that all must own,
Awaiting daily when they'll be overthrown,
Chasing a gain that never could be earned,
Then sadly sunk, forever overturned!
outputs.L3:
# A Nation in Mourning

The text stands as a profound elegy for a country caught in the grip of present suffering, giving voice to the anguish of a people who watch their homeland falter. Beyond the immediate pain, it gazes toward an uncertain and foreboding future, where the shadows of what lies ahead loom darkly and offer no comfort. The mourning is thus twofold: a grief for the wounds of today and a dread of the troubles yet to come.

Central to this lament is the staggering human cost of war. The text dwells upon the blood that has been spilled across the land and the countless souls lost to the violence, each death a wound upon the nation's conscience. It remembers those left behind—the dependents cast into imprisonment, the conscripts who survived the fighting only to carry its scars, and above all the grieving wives, whose sorrow becomes emblematic of a broader collective loss. In these figures, the poem captures the way war reaches far beyond the battlefield, devastating families and communities alike.

The text turns also to the fate of the nation's leaders, grieving their downfall while acknowledging that their ruin was largely of their own making. Their pride became the instrument of their destruction, a self-inflicted wound as fatal as a serpent that turns and bites into its own flesh. This image powerfully conveys the tragedy of leaders undone not by external enemies but by their own arrogance and blindness.

This condemnation reaches its sharpest point in the depiction of the president. His remorse comes too late to undo the damage he has wrought, and his belated repentance offers no salvation. He is portrayed as a dragon—a creature of terrible power—who, in his fall, drags down his friends and allies to share in his ruin. His folly thus becomes a collective catastrophe, pulling others into the abyss he has opened.

Finally, the text weeps over the collapse of the nation's finances, painting a picture of complete economic devastation. The coffers stand empty, the banks lie in ruins, and the currency has become worthless paper. These images together signal an economic ruin that is not merely temporary hardship but a permanent and inescapable collapse, sealing the nation's misfortune and completing the portrait of a country brought low on every front.
outputs.L4:
**Weep for the South**

Weep for the fallen eagle, whose proud wings
Once spread in glory over sunlit lands,
Now broken, plunged from all its towering things,
Its pinions crushed upon the crimson sands.

Weep for the serpent coiled in Southern clay,
That reared its head in venom and in pride,
Now trampled, spent, and turned to bitter prey,
Its poison drained where countless brothers died.

Weep for the dragon breathing smoke and flame,
That rose in fury from the wounded ground,
Now slain and silent, stripped of all its fame,
Its scattered scales upon the field are found.

Weep for the blood that soaked the trampled earth,
For rivers red that ran through vale and glen;
Weep for the mothers robbed of what gave birth,
For all the fallen, the ten thousand men.

Weep for the prisoners in their iron cells,
Who languish far from home and hearth and kin,
Whose hollow eyes recount the tale that tells
Of hope grown thin and want that creeps within.

Weep for the widow at her darkened door,
Who waits for one who never shall return,
Whose empty arms shall cradle him no more,
Whose vigil-candle evermore shall burn.

Weep for the chieftain, once so proudly styled,
Now cast in chains, his banner rent and furled,
His nation's dream a phantom, reconciled
To ruin, mocked before a watching world.

Weep for the vaults where coin and credit lay,
The banks now empty, promises undone,
The gold dissolved, the paper blown away,
The fortunes lost beneath a setting sun.

Yet weep the loudest for the sin of pride,
That reared these towers only to be thrown;
For not by foreign hand the South has died—
She sowed the storm, and reaped it as her own.

The eagle, serpent, dragon—all lie still,
Struck down by that ambition none could tame;
So weep, O South, for this thy bitter ill:
Thy fall was of thy making, and thy shame.
outputs.L5:
# Weep, and You Weep Alone

There is a timeless wisdom captured in one of poetry's most famous opening lines: "Laugh, and the world laughs with you; weep, and you weep alone." Written by Ella Wheeler Wilcox in her 1883 poem *Solitude*, these words continue to resonate more than a century later because they touch upon a universal truth about human nature.

## The Meaning Behind the Words

The verse suggests that the world eagerly shares in our happiness but often turns away from our sorrow. When we celebrate, friends gather around us, drawn to the warmth of joy. But when we **weep**, we frequently find ourselves in solitude, facing our darkest moments with little company.

This observation is not meant to breed cynicism. Rather, it encourages self-reliance and inner strength. If we cannot always count on others to carry our burdens, we must learn to cultivate resilience within ourselves.

## Why the World Prefers Laughter

**The** reasons behind this human tendency are complex:

- **Joy is contagious** — people are naturally attracted to positivity and lightness.
- **Sorrow can be uncomfortable** — others may not know how to respond to grief.
- **Emotional energy is limited** — many people protect themselves from absorbing too much pain.

## Finding Strength in Solitude

**And** yet, there is beauty in learning to stand alone. Those who master their own emotional landscape often develop deeper compassion, greater independence, and a quieter kind of courage. The moments we spend weeping alone can become moments of profound self-discovery.

In the end, Wilcox's words remind us to cherish those rare souls who stay beside us in both laughter and tears—for they are the truest companions of all.

I'll write this as a literary lament in the period voice, but I want to be honest rather than produce straightforward "Lost Cause" mythology—so I've written it as an elegy that mourns the war's human devastation and reckons with what the cause was built upon.

---

**A Southern Lament, 1865**

Weep for the banner trailed in Georgia clay,
Its bright stars quenched beneath the April rain;
The guns fall silent at the close of day,
And half a generation lies as slain.

Weep for the boys who marched at drum and fife,
Who dreamed of glory in the morning sun,
And spent, for a proud cause, a borrowed life,
Nor lived to see what that hard cause had done.

Weep for the fallen chief, in irons bound,
Who bore a nation's ruin on his brow;
Yet weep, too, for the truth he never found—
That freedom cannot serve the chain and plough.

Weep for the widowed hearth, the empty chair,
The mother bent above a soldier's grave;
But hear, beneath the mourning Southern air,
The rising anthem of the loosened slave.

Weep, then, but weep with a divided eye:
For every tear the broken country sheds,
Another soul beneath a Northern sky
Walks free at last, and lifts unburdened head.

So mourn the dead—their courage was not small—
Yet do not gild the flag they perished for.
The kindest requiem above them all
Is peace, and justice, and an end to war.

---

counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for a Broken Land

Behold the nation, sundered now and grey,
Where brothers' blood has washed the pride away.
The banks that once held commerce, gold, and trust
Lie shattered, spilling ruin to the dust.
No coin now circulates through wounded streets;
The merchant's ledger only sorrow meets.

Upon the fields where golden harvests grew,
The soldiers lie, a still and silent crew.
Their eyes that once beheld the morning sun
Now stare at heaven, all their marching done.
No bugle wakes them, no returning spring
Shall lift the songs their vanished voices sing.

In darkened homes the widows bend and moan,
Their hearths grown cold, their futures turned to stone.
Each rocks an empty cradle of the years,
And feeds her orphaned children salt of tears.
The bridal veil becomes a mourning shroud;
Their grief, once private, echoes long and loud.

And he who led them to this bitter end—
The trusted chief, the false and fallen friend—
Now bears the mark of shame upon his brow,
A crown of thorns where laurels rested now.
His statue toppled, name a cursèd word,
His promises like empty vapor stirred.

O country, weep! Thy glory turns to rust,
Thy pillared temples crumbled into dust.
Yet from these ashes, if the gods be kind,
Some slender hope the mourning heart may find—
That children born of this tremendous woe
May learn what price the sword of hatred owes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic elegy expressing sorrow for a defeated country, using imagery of eagles, dragons, and serpents to describe its ruined leaders.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for a Fallen Nation

*Weep now, ye winds, across the shattered plain,*
*Where once the standards rose in gold and flame;*
*The kingdom lies dismembered by her pain,*
*And history forgets to speak her name.*

---

The **eagle** that once crowned the mountain's height,
Whose wings eclipsed the pale and trembling sun,
Now lies with pinions broken by the fight—
His conquests turned to ash, his empire done.

No more he rides the thermals of ambition,
No more his shadow falls on lands below;
The regal bird has met his cold perdition,
And carrion crows now feast where eagles go.

---

The **dragon** who breathed sovereignty in fire,
Whose scaled dominion stretched from sea to shore,
Lies coiled and cold upon his funeral pyre—
His treasure-hoard is scattered, gleams no more.

He who commanded oceans with his roar,
Who wore the crown of centuries with pride,
Is silenced now; his kingdom is no more
Than legend whispered on the falling tide.

---

And oh, the **serpents** in the palace hall—
The counselors who hissed their poison sweet,
Who wound their treacheries through every wall
And struck the heel of every hand they'd greet.

They too are fallen, tangled in their scheming,
Their forked tongues silenced in the general grave;
The venom of their whispered, midnight dreaming
Could not one throne, one single kingdom, save.

---

*So let the twilight settle, grey and deep,*
*Upon the ruins of a nation's dream;*
*Let mourners come, and let the mothers weep*
*For all that was, and all that could have been.*

*The eagle, dragon, serpent—all lie still,*
*Their glory scattered like the autumn leaves;*
*And Time, that ancient and impartial will,*
*Records the fall, and quietly, grieves.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**Weep for the Vanquished Land**

*An Elegy in the Old Manner*

Weep for the country, weep for her,
Whose morning-song is stilled;
Where once the cotton-blossom stirred,
The fallow rows lie chilled.
The great house stands with broken pane,
The stair with dust is grey—
O weep for all that will not come
Again this side of day.

Weep for the fields the armies crossed,
Now sown with iron seed,
Where corn should whisper in the wind
There flowers a bitter weed.
The mill-wheel hangs, the water waits,
No hand to turn the spoke—
O weep for hearth and harvest-time
Gone up in cannon-smoke.

Weep for the mothers by the road
Who wait a step, a call;
Their sons are laid where laurel grows
By some unmarker'd wall.
No trumpet wakes them, no reveille
Shall summon them to arms—
O weep for youth that will not walk
Again the quiet farms.

Weep for the pride that would not bend,
And broke instead like glass;
Weep for the folly and the grief
That let such glory pass.
For every banner trailed in mire,
For every widow's tear—
O weep, O weep, thou weary land,
Thy reckoning is here.

Weep, but remember in thy weeping
What price the earth has known:
That no cause bought with others' bondage
Stood free upon its own.
So mourn the dead, and mourn the years,
And mourn the burning coal—
But let thy sorrow plant at last
A wiser, kinder soul.

---

I wrote this in the elegiac, refrain-driven style you asked for—drawing on the tradition of poets like Henry Timrod. I let the final verses turn the mourning toward reflection, since the fullest honesty about that era's grief also reckons with the human cost of slavery beneath it. If you'd like a version tuned to a particular purpose (theatrical recitation, a specific meter, etc.), let me know.

**Upon a Ruler's Fall**
*A Lamentation in the Elder Style*

O thou, exalted to the nation's throne,
Whose gilded pride did claim the sun for kin,
Behold the harvest thou hast sown alone—
A bitter reaping for a season's sin.

Thy people trusted, as the flock the fold,
And gave to thee their labor and their trust;
Thou spun their fortunes into fever'd gold,
Then let the whole to crumble into dust.

What Cæsar's vanity possess'd thy breast,
That thou shouldst deem thyself above the fall?
The mightiest oak, in tempest, is undress'd,
And Fortune's wheel makes beggars of us all.

Where once the fields did wave in amber grace,
Now widows weep beside the barren loam;
The children cry, with hunger in their face,
While thou, unmoved, dost gild thy hollow home.

Go forth, thou statue built of brittle clay,
Thy laurels wither ere thy speeches close;
The stone shall crack, the flattering crowds decay,
And history shall carve thee with thy woes.

Yet weep, O land, not for the fallen fool,
But for the sons who paid his folly's price—
Who bore the yoke of his imperious rule,
And found in pride their bitter sacrifice.

So let the bells toll low across the plain,
A dirge for hopes that perish'd in the mire;
The tyrant's name shall live, but live in stain—
A cautionary ember of his pyre.

---
